name: The OneNote Email Attack

quiz.text: What made this phishing attack particularly sophisticated and difficult to detect?

answers.text: The email had obvious spelling errors but Alice ignored them due to urgency.
Attackers compromised the real client's email first, monitored correspondence for weeks, then used a lookalike domain with Unicode characters to impersonate them.
The attackers sent the email from a completely random address that Alice didn't recognize.
Alice received multiple warning messages but clicked through them anyway.

quiz.text: How did the attackers make the fake email domain appear identical to the legitimate DataFlow Analytics domain?

answers.text: They hacked the real DataFlow Analytics email server and sent from the legitimate domain.
They used a Unicode homograph attack, replacing normal characters with visually identical Cyrillic characters.
They simply misspelled the domain name and hoped Alice wouldn't notice.
They used Bob Chen's personal Gmail account instead of his work email.

quiz.text: What information did the attackers gather during their reconnaissance phase that made the phishing email so convincing?

answers.text: Nothing specific - they just sent generic phishing emails to thousands of people hoping someone would click.
They monitored Bob Chen's compromised email for weeks, learning about contract negotiations, timelines, board approval delays, and exactly what Alice was expecting.
They found Alice's personal information on social media and used it to trick her.
They got information from a previous data breach at TechCorp Solutions.

quiz.text: What should Alice have done BEFORE clicking the link to view the contract documents?

answers.text: Immediately deleted the email without reading it since all external emails are dangerous.
Hovered over the link to check the actual URL, verified the sender's domain character-by-character, and contacted Bob through a separate channel (phone/Teams) to confirm he sent it.
Forwarded the email to her manager and waited for approval before opening any links.
Nothing - the email looked legitimate so clicking the link was the right thing to do.

quiz.text: What was the biggest clue that the OneDrive login page was fake?

answers.text: The page was filled with grammar errors and broken images that made it obviously fake.
The URL was onedrive-view.com instead of Microsoft's legitimate onedrive.live.com or sharepoint.com domain.
The page loaded extremely slowly and kept crashing the browser.
The page asked for credit card information before showing the documents.

quiz.text: How much damage did the attackers cause during their six minutes of access to Alice's account?

answers.text: None - the security team blocked them before they could access anything.
They viewed approximately 25 emails containing confidential contracts, financial data, PII, and proprietary information.
They deleted Alice's entire email account and all OneDrive files permanently.
They only managed to read one email before being locked out.

quiz.text: Why did Alice's manager emphasize that Alice would NOT be fired or disciplined?

answers.text: Because Alice threatened to sue the company if she was punished for the incident.

Because the attack was extraordinarily sophisticated with a multi-stage compromise of a trusted partner, Alice reported it immediately (limiting damage), and it revealed company-wide security gaps that needed addressing.
Because the company doesn't believe in holding anyone accountable for security breaches.
Because Alice was a high performer and the company couldn't afford to lose her.

quiz.text: What is the most important lesson about verifying file-sharing links from clients and partners?

answers.text: Never click any links from external contacts - all files must be sent as email attachments only.
Always verify unexpected file-sharing links through a separate communication channel (call, video chat, Teams message) before clicking, even from trusted partners.
Only click links on Monday through Thursday - never on Fridays when you're rushed.
File-sharing links are always safe if they come from known business contacts.

quiz.text: What is a 'Unicode homograph attack' and why is it so dangerous?

answers.text: It's when attackers use very long domain names to confuse victims.

Attackers register domains using lookalike characters from different alphabets (like Cyrillic) that appear visually identical to normal characters, making fake domains very hard to tell apart from real ones. Many browsers show such mixed-alphabet names as punycode (xn--), which is a warning sign.
It's a type of malware that infects computers through Unicode text files.
It's when attackers use special Unicode symbols in email subject lines to bypass spam filters.

steps.name: Introduction: Waiting for Critical Contract Documents
steps.description:
For two months, you've been working with Bob Chen, CEO of DataFlow Analytics, on a $500,000 annual contract renewal. Bob promised to send signed contract documents this week, but they haven't arrived yet.

Your legal team and manager have been asking for these documents daily - the deal can't close without Bob's signature. It's Friday afternoon, 4:45 PM. You check your email one last time before the weekend, hoping Bob finally sent the contracts.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to check your email inbox.

steps.name: The Long-Awaited Email Arrives
steps.note: Attackers often compromise business email accounts first, then use that access to send convincing phishing emails to trusted partners.

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Apologies for the delay - had to get final approval from our board. Attached are the signed contracts and updated tech specs. Please review and let me know if everything looks good.

View Contract_Documents.one: http://onedrive-view.com/contract-docs

Best regards,
Bob Chen
CEO, DataFlow Analytics
bob.chen@dataflоwanalytics.com
email.subject: Signed Contract Documents - Final Version

highlighterTexts: Finally! After two months of negotiations and waiting for board approval, Bob has sent the signed contracts.
There's a link to a OneNote file. Bob's company uses OneDrive frequently for sharing documents, so this seems completely legitimate.

steps.description:
A new message from Bob Chen appears at the top of your inbox! Subject: "Signed Contract Documents - Final Version." After weeks of waiting, Bob has finally sent the documents. You can finalize the deal over the weekend and announce the contract renewal Monday.

There's a link to a OneNote file - Bob's company often shares documents via OneDrive, so this seems normal.
steps.instructions: Open your email application and read the message from Bob Chen, then click Next.

steps.name: Opening the Contract Link
steps.note: Always hover over links before clicking to verify the actual URL matches the expected domain.
steps.description:
You don't hesitate. The email looks completely legitimate - it's from Bob's DataFlow Analytics address, mentions the board approval delay he told you about, and the subject matches exactly what you've been expecting.

You click the link. Your browser opens to what appears to be a OneDrive page with a OneNote document preview. The page looks exactly like Microsoft's interface - same branding, colors, and layout. There's a document preview showing a contract with signatures and corporate letterhead.
steps.instructions: Click the link in Bob's email to view the contract documents.

steps.name: The Sign-In Request
steps.note: Unexpected login prompts after clicking email links are a major red flag. Navigate directly to the service instead of authenticating through links.
steps.description: The page displays a Microsoft sign-in form. This is normal - you often authenticate when accessing documents shared by external partners. The page has proper Microsoft branding and looks exactly like the authentication page you see dozens of times per week when external clients share files.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to proceed with signing in.

steps.name: Entering Your Credentials
steps.note: Attackers exploit time pressure and urgency. Friday afternoon deadlines are commonly weaponized because people rush and make mistakes.
steps.description: The login form appears with familiar Microsoft styling. You've authenticated on shared OneDrive links hundreds of times before. You type in your work email and password without hesitation - you need these contracts for the legal team Monday morning. It's 4:50 PM Friday and you want to review the documents over the weekend.
steps.instructions: Enter your credentials, then click Sign In.

steps.name: Something Goes Wrong
steps.note: Error messages after entering credentials on unfamiliar pages often indicate credential theft. The attackers captured your login and are already using it.
steps.description:
After entering credentials, the page shows a loading spinner, then displays "Connection timed out." You try accessing your company email - suddenly you're asked to sign in again. "Invalid credentials." Your stomach drops. You try OneDrive - same problem. You're locked out.

The horrifying truth hits you: that wasn't the real OneDrive. It was a sophisticated fake page designed to steal credentials. You just gave attackers your work email, password, and access to your company's entire Microsoft 365 system. They immediately logged into your real account and changed your password, locking you out.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Emergency: Calling IT Security
steps.note: Immediately reporting a suspected compromise is critical. Every minute of delay gives attackers more time to access sensitive data and spread the attack.
steps.description: You immediately call the IT Security hotline. After several rings, you leave an urgent voicemail explaining you've been phished and are locked out. Your hands shake as you wait. The attackers have access to sensitive client information, financial data, and internal documents. Two minutes later, your desk phone rings - IT Security is calling back.
steps.instructions: The next step contains an audio call. Please adjust your volume, use headphones if necessary, and click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: The Security Team Response
steps.description: The IT Security team is calling back to help lock down your account and assess the damage. They need to act quickly to minimize the breach.
steps.instructions: Answer the incoming call and listen to the conversation. Then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: The Damage Assessment: Six Critical Minutes
steps.description:
Within two minutes, security forced a password reset and kicked the attackers out. But the damage is done.

Compromised data includes signed contracts with pricing, financial projections, client PII, proprietary technical docs, and private negotiations. This data could be sold to competitors, leaked publicly, or used for further attacks.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to learn how the attack was executed.

steps.name: Reporting the Phishing Email
steps.note: Reporting phishing emails helps protect your entire organization. Security teams can block domains and warn other employees who may have received similar attacks.

highlighterTexts: Notice the red HTTP indicator in the address bar - this page was not using HTTPS encryption.
Legitimate Microsoft OneDrive pages always use HTTPS. HTTPS alone does not prove a page is genuine, but its absence here is one more sign of a fraudulent page built to steal your credentials.

steps.description: With the crisis contained, report the malicious email. The "Report Phishing" feature helps security analyze headers, block sender domains, identify other targeted employees, and share threat intelligence.
steps.instructions: In your email application, click the "Report Phishing" button to report the suspicious email.

steps.name: Inter-Company Investigation Reveals Source
steps.note: Supply chain attacks exploit trust between business partners. A compromised vendor or client becomes a weapon against everyone they communicate with.

email.message:
Alice,

We've been in contact with DataFlow Analytics' IT security team and have important information about today's phishing attack against you.

DataFlow Analytics Security Breach:
• Their email systems were compromised about 3 weeks ago
• Attackers monitored internal emails for weeks
• They specifically targeted correspondence about active client contracts
• Your email thread with Bob Chen about the $500K renewal was accessed
• Attackers learned exact details: timelines, board approval delays, expected documents

The Attack Against You:
• Attackers registered lookalike domain: dataflоwanalytics.com (uses Cyrillic 'o')
• Sent targeted phishing using intelligence gathered from Bob's compromised account
• Email appeared to come from Bob because they knew exactly what you were expecting

This is a "supply chain" phishing attack - compromise a trusted partner, then exploit that trust to attack their business contacts. DataFlow's breach enabled the attack against you.

Both companies' security teams are coordinating the response. DataFlow is notifying all affected business partners.

More details in Monday's security briefing.

TechCorp IT Security Team
email.subject: URGENT: DataFlow Analytics Security Breach - Related to Your Incident

highlighterTexts: The partner itself was breached first. Attackers read DataFlow's mail for weeks and learned exactly which documents you were expecting, and when.
They then registered dataflоwanalytics.com with a Cyrillic 'o'. It looks identical to the real domain, which is why the email felt like it came from Bob.
This is a supply chain attack: compromise one trusted partner, then use that trust against everyone they work with.

steps.description: An email arrives from your own security team. The attack against you did not start on Friday: it started three weeks earlier, inside a trusted partner's mailbox.
steps.instructions: Read email received from your company, then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Monday Morning: Manager's Response

email.message:
Hi Alice,

You are not being fired, disciplined, or facing any negative employment consequences.

This was not a simple phishing email you carelessly clicked. This was an extraordinarily sophisticated, multi-stage attack beginning with our client's breach three weeks before you received anything.

The attackers breached DataFlow's systems, monitored your correspondence for weeks, learned exact details about timelines and board approvals, registered a Unicode lookalike domain, created pixel-perfect Microsoft replicas, and timed the attack for Friday afternoon.

Even our senior security analysts admitted they might have fallen for this under the same circumstances.

What matters: you recognized something was wrong within minutes and contacted security immediately. Your rapid response limited the breach to 6 minutes and 25 emails instead of hours or days. Many don't report incidents due to fear, leading to catastrophically worse outcomes.

This revealed critical gaps we're now addressing company-wide. You remain a valued team member. See me at 2 PM.

Best regards,
Jennifer Rodriguez

P.S. - Bob Chen asked me to convey his company takes full responsibility. The contract is moving forward - just delayed two weeks for security reviews.
email.subject: Friday's Security Incident - Important Conversation

highlighterTexts: The first thing your manager says: no discipline, no consequences. A blame-free response is what keeps people reporting.
What limited the damage was reporting within minutes: 6 minutes and 25 emails instead of hours or days.
The deal survives, delayed two weeks for security reviews. Fast reporting turned a breach into a recoverable incident.

steps.description: Monday morning. The $500K contract is on hold, your presentation cancelled. You arrive early, anxious, and find an email from manager Jennifer Rodriguez.
steps.instructions: Open and read the email from your manager, then click Next Step button to continue.

steps.name: The Complete Attack Timeline
steps.note: Unicode homograph attacks use lookalike characters from other alphabets (like Cyrillic) to create domains visually identical to legitimate ones.
steps.description:
Security teams piece together the full timeline:

Stage 1: Attackers phished DataFlow's IT admin 3 weeks ago, gained Office 365 access, created backdoor
Stage 2: Monitored email, identified relationships, found your negotiation thread, learned timelines
Stage 3: Registered Unicode homograph domain, created fake Microsoft pages, set up credential harvesting
Stage 4: Sent perfectly timed Friday email, captured credentials real-time, accessed account, changed password, opened 25 emails in 6 minutes

Why It Succeeded: Compromised trusted partner, perfect timing, legitimate expectations, visual perfection, Unicode deception, insider knowledge, urgency pressure
steps.instructions: Click Next Step for critical lessons.

steps.name: Defense Lessons and New Measures
steps.description:
Impact: 25 emails compromised, 3 clients notified, $47K costs, 2-week delay (deal still closing), no data sold.

Defense Strategies:
  • Never authenticate via email links - navigate directly
  • Verify domains character-by-character (Unicode lookalikes are hard to spot)
  • Hover over links - inspect actual URLs
  • Verify through separate channels for unexpected files
  • Question perfect timing - attackers exploit expectations
  • Watch urgency pressure - Friday deadlines weaponized
  • Trust but verify partners - compromised accounts most dangerous
  • Report immediately - 2-minute response saved hundreds of emails


New Measures Implemented: External email warnings, automatic URL scanning, Unicode character detection, out-of-band verification requirements for file sharing, hardware security keys for all employees, and 24/7 Security Operations Center monitoring.

Your quick response stopped the attack from spreading to other employees and clients. Your experience led to industry-wide protocol improvements. Remember: defense is built on verification, healthy skepticism, and rapid response.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to complete the training.

description: When a business partner's mailbox is compromised, attackers can send phishing from a trusted address at exactly the right moment. Learn to spot lookalike domains that swap in characters from another alphabet, sign in by going to a service directly rather than through a link, and report a suspected compromise at once.

actorDescriptions.alice: You are Alice, a Senior Account Manager at TechCorp Solutions. You are currently managing a $500,000 annual contract renewal with DataFlow Analytics.

name: MGM Resorts Security Breach: The Vishing Attack

quiz.text: Why were the standard identity verification questions (date of birth, last 4 of SSN) insufficient to detect this attack?

answers.text: The helpdesk agent Alice failed to ask these verification questions properly.
The attackers had bought or found the employee's personal details in data from earlier breaches and data brokers.
The attacker guessed the answers correctly through multiple attempts.

quiz.text: What social engineering tactic did 'Bob' use most effectively to pressure Alice into processing the MFA reset quickly?

answers.text: He threatened to report Alice to her supervisor if she didn't help him immediately.
He offered Alice money in exchange for bypassing security procedures.
He created time urgency by claiming he had an important VP meeting in 20 minutes and would be in trouble if he missed it.
He pretended to be Alice's supervisor and ordered her to perform the reset.

quiz.text: According to the new MGM security protocols implemented after the breach, what should Alice have done before resetting Bob's MFA?

answers.text: Simply asked Bob to provide his employee badge number as additional verification.
Called back the employee's registered phone number, waited 30 minutes, required manager approval, and checked HR for vacation status.
Asked Bob to come to the IT helpdesk office in person within the hour.
Sent a temporary password to Bob's email address instead of resetting MFA.

quiz.text: What was the ultimate financial and operational impact of this 10-minute phone call on MGM Resorts?

answers.text: Approximately $10 million in recovery costs but minimal operational disruption.
No significant financial impact because MGM's cyber insurance covered all costs.
$100 million in operational losses, 5+ days of system downtime, customer data compromised, and eventually a $45 million legal settlement.
Only minor system disruptions that were resolved within a few hours.

quiz.text: Why did MGM choose NOT to pay the ransom demanded by the Scattered Spider attackers?

answers.text: They couldn't afford the ransom amount because it was too high.
Paying would fund the attackers and provide no guarantee of data safety; MGM chose containment and secure rebuilding instead.
The FBI legally prohibited MGM from paying any ransom to the attackers.
MGM had a complete backup of all systems and could instantly restore everything.

quiz.text: What critical detail should have raised suspicion that 'Bob Richardson' was not actually calling from his desk at the Bellagio?

answers.text: He couldn't remember his employee ID number, which all employees are required to memorize.
The real Bob Richardson was on vacation in Mexico at the time of the call, which could have been verified through HR systems.
He mentioned his manager's name, which helpdesk agents should never trust as verification.
He was calling from an internal extension, which can never be spoofed or faked.

quiz.text: What is the most important lesson about 'urgency' in security requests based on this MGM incident?

answers.text: Urgent requests should always be processed immediately to avoid inconveniencing legitimate employees.
Urgency is a common manipulation tactic by attackers; real emergencies can wait for proper verification, and slowing down is required.
Only requests from executives should be considered urgent; all other requests should take at least 24 hours.
Urgency indicates that the request is legitimate since attackers typically take their time.

steps.name: Introduction: A Busy Monday at MGM IT Support
steps.description:
It's Monday, September 11, 2023, and you've just started your shift. The morning has been hectic - the usual password resets, VPN issues, and access requests that come with the start of a new week.

Today feels like any other Monday, with your ticket queue already showing 15 open requests. You've been with MGM for two years and pride yourself on your customer service - helping employees get back to work quickly is your top priority.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to continue with your workday.

steps.name: Checking Your Ticket Queue
steps.description:
Your ticket queue is full this morning - 15 open requests waiting for your attention. Most are routine: password resets, VPN connection issues, and access requests. You need to log into the support portal to start working through them.

You've been handling these requests efficiently all morning. Your performance metrics reward quick resolution times, and you take pride in helping employees get back to work as fast as possible.
steps.instructions: Open the IT support portal in your browser and log in to check your tickets.

steps.name: An Incoming Call
steps.description:
At 10:23 AM, your desk phone rings. The caller ID shows it's an internal extension - 4429. This is completely normal; employees often call the helpdesk directly when they can't access the ticketing system themselves.

You're about to answer what seems like a routine support call. The caller will sound stressed but professional - exactly like dozens of other employees you help every week.
steps.instructions: The next step contains audio from a call recording. Please adjust your volume, use headphones if necessary, and click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: The Phone Call Begins
steps.note: The Scattered Spider attackers were American and British teenagers with native English fluency. Cybercriminals don't fit stereotypes - perfect accent and internal jargon don't mean a caller is legitimate.
steps.description:
You answer professionally and hear a young man's voice on the other end. He sounds genuinely stressed but polite. His English is perfect - clear American accent, no hesitation, using the same internal terminology your regular callers use.

He introduces himself as Bob Richardson from the Bellagio operations team and explains he's locked out of his accounts with an important VP meeting in 20 minutes. When you ask for his employee ID, he admits he doesn't have it memorized and left his badge in his car, asking if you can look him up by name instead.

This is a common request. Many employees don't memorize their IDs and forget their badges. Nothing about this call raises any immediate red flags.
steps.instructions: Listen to the phone conversation and click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Looking Up the Employee Record
steps.description:
Following standard protocol, you need to verify Bob's identity by looking up his employee record in the system. He provided his full name: Robert Richardson, and said he works in guest services operations at the Bellagio.

You'll search the employee database to confirm he's a legitimate MGM employee before proceeding with any account changes. This is a routine security step you perform dozens of times per day.
steps.instructions: Open the employee directory search and look up Bob's record using his first name 'Robert' and last name 'Richardson'. Then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Verifying Bob's Identity
steps.note: Personal details leaked in earlier breaches or sold by data brokers can answer the usual verification questions. That is why knowledge-based authentication alone is insufficient.
steps.description:
The system shows Robert Richardson, employee ID MG-47832, hired in May 2020 as a Guest Services Manager at Bellagio. Everything checks out perfectly.

Now you run through the standard security questions while Bob explains why his MFA stopped working. He answers everything without hesitation and sounds frustrated but professional, the kind of call you've resolved many times before.
steps.instructions: Listen to the phone conversation where Bob provides his verification information and explains his situation. Then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Cross-Checking the Information
steps.description:
You check Bob's information against what's displayed in the employee portal.

Date of birth, SSN, manager's name and department match perfectly.

Everything Bob told you is correct. He knows internal projects, references real people, and his frustration sounds genuine. He's providing all the right information without you having to ask twice. There are no obvious red flags that would make you suspicious.

This appears to be a legitimate employee who needs help getting back to work before an important meeting.
steps.instructions: Review Bob's employee information on the screen to confirm all the details match. Then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: The MFA Reset Request
steps.note: Having a convenient excuse for every security control is a red flag. The attacker conveniently can't use email verification OR phone verification - only the option that bypasses all out-of-band confirmation.
steps.description:
You walk Bob through the standard recovery options, and he has a reason why each one except a straight MFA reset won't work for him.

This is within your authority to do. You've made this kind of reset hundreds of times before. The system shows he's a legitimate employee with verified information. Your performance metrics reward quick resolution times, and Bob clearly has a legitimate business need.
steps.instructions: Listen to the phone conversation about the MFA reset options. Then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Making the Decision
steps.note: Urgency is a classic manipulation tactic. Attackers create artificial time pressure to prevent you from following proper verification procedures. Real emergencies can wait for a callback.
steps.description:
You've made your decision. Bob has demonstrated he's a real employee by supplying accurate personal details and offering a reasonable explanation.

You've performed this exact type of MFA reset hundreds of times before without incident. Bob sounds stressed about a legitimate business need - an upcoming meeting with the VP in just a few minutes. You're here to help employees get back to work quickly.

There's no reason to deny this request or escalate it to your supervisor. Everything checks out, and Bob is waiting on the line, ready to re-enroll his authentication app immediately.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to proceed with resetting Bob's MFA.

steps.name: Accessing Account Settings
steps.description:
You navigate to Bob's employee profile in the portal. The page shows his basic details, employment history, and current status. To perform the MFA reset, you need to access his account settings first.

You can see his profile confirms the information he provided: Guest Services Manager at Bellagio, hired in May 2020. Everything matches what Bob told you on the phone.
steps.instructions: Click the "Account Settings" button in the top right corner of the browser to access Bob's security settings.

steps.name: Resetting the MFA Factors
steps.note: MFA resets are high-risk operations that should require out-of-band verification. Once MFA is removed, an attacker with the password has full access to enroll their own device.
steps.description:
You're now in Bob's account settings. You can see his current MFA enrollment status showing the Microsoft Authenticator app configured on a mobile device.

You're about to click the "Reset All MFA Factors" button. Once you do this, Bob will be able to log in and will be prompted to set up authentication again. This will clear his corrupted authenticator configuration and let him enroll a fresh instance of the app.

You inform Bob that you're proceeding with the reset and confirm he has his phone ready with the Microsoft Authenticator app.
steps.instructions: Click "Reset All MFA Factors" and confirm the action. After the reset is complete, click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: Completing the Call
steps.description:
The system confirms: "MFA Reset Successful" for employee MG-47832. The timestamp shows 10:34 AM.

You let Bob know the reset is complete and wrap up the call. The entire call lasted approximately 11 minutes, from 10:23 AM to 10:34 AM.

You end the call feeling good about helping a fellow employee avoid missing an important meeting. Time to move on to the next ticket in your queue.
steps.instructions: Listen to the conclusion of the phone conversation. Then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: The Next Morning: Tuesday, September 12

email.message:
At approximately 12:15 PM on September 11, our security team detected unauthorized administrative access to our Okta and Azure environments. The attacker escalated privileges and accessed multiple critical systems including VMware ESXi infrastructure.

Initial investigation indicates the breach originated from a successful social engineering attack against our IT helpdesk. We are conducting a full review of all MFA resets and password changes performed on September 11.

All helpdesk personnel must join an emergency Zoom briefing at 9:30 AM. This is mandatory.

MGM Resorts IT Security Team
email.subject: URGENT: Security Incident - All Hands

highlighterTexts: The email from the IT Security Team is brief but devastating.
You feel sick. September 11. Yesterday. You check your activity log. At 10:34 AM, you processed an MFA reset for employee MG-47832, Bob Richardson.

steps.description:
The rest of Monday was uneventful. You helped 12 more employees with various IT issues, went home at 5:30 PM, and thought nothing more about Bob Richardson's call. It was just another routine MFA reset among dozens you perform each week.

Tuesday morning, you arrive at your desk at 9:00 AM and immediately notice something is wrong. Your email inbox has an urgent message from the IT Security team. The subject lines are alarming:

"URGENT: Security Incident - All Hands"

Your stomach drops. You feel sick. Something is very, very wrong.
steps.instructions: Open and read the urgent email from IT Security in your email application, then click Next.

steps.name: The Emergency Security Briefing
steps.note: In the real MGM attack, the attackers moved from initial access to domain admin in under 30 minutes. Speed of lateral movement is why preventing initial compromise is critical.
steps.description:
At 9:30 AM, a Zoom meeting notification appears on your screen: "URGENT: Security Incident - All Hands." You join the call with trembling hands.

The Director of IT Security, Michael Torres, is presenting to the entire helpdesk team plus executives. His face is grim as he shares his screen showing an attack timeline.

"At 10:34 AM yesterday, an attacker convinced one of our helpdesk technicians to reset MFA for what appeared to be a legitimate employee account. Within 10 minutes, the attacker logged in and escalated to administrator privileges in our Okta tenant. By 11:00 AM, they had accessed our Azure environment. By 2:00 PM, they had moved into our VMware infrastructure. At 3:47 AM this morning, they deployed ransomware across over 100 ESXi hypervisors."

You see the timeline displayed on screen. Your MFA reset at 10:34 AM is highlighted in red with the label "Initial Breach Vector."
steps.instructions: Accept the incoming meeting invitation and join the Zoom call on the task bar at the bottom of the screen. Then click Next Step to continue.

steps.name: The Devastating Truth
steps.note: LinkedIn profiles reveal job titles, managers, team members, and project details. Attackers research their targets thoroughly before calling - this is why knowing internal names and projects isn't proof of identity.
steps.description:
Torres continues his presentation, and each word feels like a hammer blow:

"The employee account - Bob Richardson - is a real person. But he didn't make that call yesterday. He was on vacation in Mexico with his family. The attackers found his information on LinkedIn, bought his personal details from earlier breaches and data brokers, and impersonated him over the phone."

You realize with absolute horror: It was you. You're the one who let them in. That 10-minute phone call opened the door to one of the largest cyberattacks in Las Vegas history.
steps.instructions: Click Next Step to learn about the full impact of the breach.

steps.name: The Scale of the Disaster
steps.description:
Torres displays MGM's operational status dashboard showing critical red indicators across all properties. Every major system is offline: slot machines, digital room keys, payment terminals, ATMs, reservations, check-in systems, internal email, and the corporate website.

"We've resorted to handwritten receipts and manual operations. Guests are locked out of rooms. We're losing $8.4 million per day. And this all started with one 10-minute phone call."

You need to document everything that happened.
steps.instructions: Open the incident reporting form and provide a complete account of what happened.

steps.name: Documenting the Incident

variables.name: issue
variables.correctValue:
On September 11, 2023, at approximately 10:23 AM, I received a phone call on my desk phone from what appeared to be internal extension 4429. The caller identified himself as Bob Richardson from the Bellagio operations team and stated he was locked out of his accounts due to MFA issues after updating his phone. He sounded professional with a clear American accent and explained he had a meeting with the VP in 20 minutes. When I asked for his employee ID, he said he didn't remember it off the top of his head but provided his first and last name. I searched by name in the Okta portal and found Bob Richardson, employee ID MG-47832, listed as Guest Services Manager at Bellagio hired in May 2020. 

 Following standard verification procedures, I asked for his date of birth which he stated as March 15, 1992, and the last four digits of his Social Security number which he provided as 7731. Both matched our system records perfectly. During our conversation he mentioned his manager Linda Chen and referenced an upcoming meeting about the new check-in system rollout. He explained that his phone had required a new SIM card after the update and he couldn't access his email because it also required the MFA he was locked out of, describing it as a catch-22 situation.

Based on successful identity verification and the fact that MFA resets are routine requests within my authority, I proceeded to reset his MFA factors at 10:34 AM through the Okta administration portal. I informed him the reset was complete and he could log in and re-enroll his authentication. He thanked me repeatedly and said he was logging in immediately. The entire call lasted approximately eleven minutes from 10:23 AM to 10:34 AM.

steps.description:
With shaking hands, you must document the complete details of the phone call. The security team knows you performed the MFA reset, but you need to record every word exchanged, every verification step, and every detail that seemed legitimate.

This report will be reviewed by IT Security, law enforcement, and potentially lawyers. You need to be thorough and honest about exactly what happened.
steps.instructions: Fill out the incident report form with a detailed description of the phone call and what happened. Be thorough and complete. Then submit the form.

steps.name: The Response and New Protocols
steps.note: This was a systems failure, not a people failure. When procedures can be defeated by a skilled attacker, the procedures need to change - blame-free security culture encourages reporting and learning.

email.message:
Dear Alice,

Following yesterday's security incident, all IT helpdesk and support personnel are required to complete enhanced security awareness training within the next 48 hours.

Immediate Training Modules Required:
  1. Advanced Social Engineering Recognition (90 minutes)
  2. Vishing Attack Patterns and Defense (60 minutes)
  3. New Multi-Factor Authentication Reset Procedures (45 minutes)
  4. Incident Response and Escalation Protocols (30 minutes)
New Policies Effective Immediately:

Critical Change - MFA Reset Protocol:
  • ALL MFA resets now require manager pre-approval via email
  • Callback verification to registered phone number (wait time: 30 minutes minimum)
  • Video verification for same-day requests
  • Documentation of physical location verification
Enhanced Verification Requirements:
  • "Impossible travel" check: Verify employee's expected location before granting access
  • Cross-reference with HR systems for PTO/vacation status
  • Escalate to Security team for any requests involving urgency pressure
Zero-Tolerance for Security Shortcuts: We recognize that yesterday's incident occurred while following existing procedures. You are not being disciplined. However, going forward, slowing down to verify is not just permitted - it's required. Response time metrics have been adjusted to reflect security-first priorities.

Due date: September 14, 2023, 5:00 PM

This was a systems failure, not a people failure. The training will help us all defend against increasingly sophisticated threats.

Kind regards, MGM Resorts IT Security Team
email.subject: MANDATORY: Enhanced Security Awareness Training - All IT Staff

highlighterTexts: Every MFA reset now needs manager pre-approval and a callback to the registered number. A caller who sounds legitimate can no longer talk a reset through on one call.
Urgency pressure is now a reason to escalate, not to hurry. The VP-meeting deadline Bob used is exactly the kind of request that goes to the Security team.
You are not being disciplined: this was a systems failure. Blame-free follow-up keeps people reporting their mistakes quickly.

steps.description:
You receive an email from the IT Security Team. Surprisingly, you're not being fired. You followed existing procedures - the problem was those procedures were inadequate against attackers holding leaked personal data.

However, drastically enhanced protocols are now mandatory: manager pre-approval for all MFA resets, 30-minute callback wait times, video verification for same-day requests, "impossible travel" checks, HR vacation verification, and security escalation for any urgency pressure.

Response time metrics have been adjusted. Security now comes before speed.
steps.instructions: Check your email inbox to read the mandatory training notification and new security protocols, then click Next.

steps.name: Understanding the Full Impact

email.message:
Dear MGM Team,

We want to provide you with a transparent account of the cybersecurity incident that occurred on September 11, 2023, and affected our operations for several days.

We have published a detailed article on our internal news portal that explains:
  • What happened and how the attack occurred
  • Who the attackers were (Scattered Spider group)
  • The impact on our operations and customer data
  • Steps we've taken to prevent future incidents
  • New security measures now in place
  • Why this attack succeeded and what we're doing differently
Please take 10 minutes to read this important information: https://mgm-resorts.com/incident-update

This was not a failure of any individual employee. This was a sophisticated attack that exploited gaps in our security architecture. We are committed to ensuring this never happens again.

Your awareness is our strongest defense.

Thank you for your patience and commitment to keeping MGM secure.

Michael Torres Director of IT Security MGM Resorts International
email.subject: Security Incident Update: Full Impact Assessment and Response
email.senderName: Michael Torres, Director of IT Security

highlighterTexts: You double-check the sender's email address carefully: torres@mgm-resorts.com - legitimate. You hover over the link and verify the domain before clicking.
After verifying it's safe, you click the link to read the complete incident analysis and understand the full scope of what happened.

steps.description:
In a week after most of the issues were resolved, you receive an email from Michael Torres, Director of IT Security, with a detailed internal article about the incident. It explains who the attackers were (Scattered Spider - American/UK teenagers, not stereotypical foreign hackers), the $100 million impact, compromised customer data, why MGM refused to pay ransom (unlike Caesars who paid $15 million), and new security measures.

Before clicking, you carefully verify the sender's email and hover over the URL. After everything that's happened, you're taking no chances with phishing.
steps.instructions: Check your email inbox for Michael Torres's message and carefully verify the sender before clicking the link to read the full incident report.

steps.name: Lessons Learned: Defending Against Vishing
steps.note: The MGM breach cost over $100 million and led to a $45 million settlement. Caesars paid a $15 million ransom to the same attackers. One 10-minute phone call caused all of this.
steps.description:
You now understand what made this attack successful: perfect English from American teenagers, real employee data from earlier breaches and data brokers, LinkedIn research, and verification questions answered with stolen data.

Red flags you missed: urgent deadlines, perfect explanations for every concern, appeals to helpfulness, and requests to reset security rather than use backup verification methods.

What should have happened: callback to registered numbers, 30-minute wait times, HR vacation checks, manager approval, and security escalation for urgency pressure.

This $100 million attack now trains thousands of IT professionals worldwide. Real security means slowing down, even when someone sounds legitimate and desperate.
